description: A licensed Florida contractor's WordPress site rebuilt as ten static Next.js routes: 94% less homepage weight, 70% faster mobile paint, SEO 77 to 100. The crawl found four systemic zeroes: no page had a meta description, structured data, a share image or any analytics. The homepage carried 29MB, painted in 11.6 seconds, and rendered 435px wide inside a 390px phone. The rebuild holds the whole business in one TypeScript file that routing, the sitemap, the JSON-LD and the contact form all read from. Live since August 2026: noindex lifted, all ten routes serving, share image shipped.

highlights.title: Measured, Not Estimated
highlights.summary: Two Lighthouse 12.8.2 runs, same machine, same day: the live WordPress site and the production build. Server response time excluded; hosted and local aren't comparable.

highlights.title: The Four Zeroes

highlights.title: Rankings Carried, Not Dumped
highlights.summary: Five services retired. The two whose scope moved redirect to the pages that absorbed them, copy verbatim; a 301 into a list throws away the intent that earned the ranking.

highlights.title: The Misspelling That Cost a Keyword

highlights.title: What Is Not Done
highlights.summary: Privacy policy and terms still return 404 on the live site, and a duplicate domain sits with the client. The launch cleared the share image off this list.

result: Fifteen pages became ten, four systemic zeroes became one, and every figure was measured on the same machine on the same day, including the three that moved the wrong way.

title: Zahav Medspa
subtitle: Medical Spa in North Scottsdale, Arizona

metrics.label: visits end in a book-appointment click (GA4, Jul–Aug 2026)

description: Zahav Medspa competes in North Scottsdale aesthetics, where every rival buys the same keywords and runs the same ads. We rebuilt the brand, the site and the search foundation underneath it, then graded the result with Google's own tooling instead of our own. Google now scores the site 99/100 on performance and 100/100 on both SEO and best practices, with a perfect zero on layout shift and a one-second desktop load. On mobile, where the site was worst, the homepage went from a 13.5-second load to roughly seven, and the products page from fifteen seconds to under six. Twenty-five pages carried no H1 at all and thirty-five images had no alt text; both are now zero. The media library was cut by more than half. Average search position has climbed from 25 to 21 and is still moving, and the practice ranks in the top two for "medical spa troon north scottsdale" and "best medical spa near me". Nearly every figure here is a Google score you can re-run against zahavmedspa.com in about thirty seconds, which is the point. The one that isn't comes from the site's own analytics and is labelled as such: across July and August 2026, one visit in thirteen ended in a book-appointment click. We would rather publish numbers you can check than numbers you have to take on faith.

description: Scout is a Switch Case Studio product: commercial-real-estate scouting sold as a monthly retainer. It watches the broker sites and listing feeds a tenant would otherwise check by hand, pulls every matching lease listing into one board, and scores each against the client's own profile: geography, size, use type, demographics, co-tenancy, competition. highlights.title: One board, every source

title: Jelly Belly Wiki
subtitle: Python scraper → MySQL → C# / .NET API → React client. A four-stage data pipeline, built solo.

metrics.label: scraper, database, API and front end by one developer

description: Jelly Belly Wiki is a data pipeline, not a website. A Python scraper pulls flavor, recipe, fact and milestone data from the official Jelly Belly site; the cleaned JSON seeds a MySQL database through Entity Framework Core migrations; a C# / ASP.NET Core API serves it over ten documented endpoints with filtering, search and pagination; and a React front end consumes that same public API, the identical one any other developer can call. Three languages, three deployment targets, one developer, and every stage still running today.
tileVersion: A four-stage data pipeline: Python scraper → MySQL → C# / .NET API → React client, with public Swagger docs. 317 records, 10 endpoints, built solo.

highlights.title: 1 · Collection · Python
highlights.summary: Selenium and BeautifulSoup scrape flavors, recipes, facts and milestones from the official Jelly Belly site, then normalise the result to clean JSON ready to seed.

highlights.title: 2 · Data model · MySQL
highlights.summary: Five related resources modelled in Entity Framework Core and seeded through migrations, so the schema rebuilds from scratch rather than being hand-loaded.

highlights.title: 3 · API · C# / ASP.NET Core
highlights.summary: Ten read endpoints serving 317 records, with filtering, search and paginated responses built on LINQ queries.

highlights.title: 4 · Documentation · Swagger
highlights.summary: A live, interactive Swagger UI plus in-app documentation, so another developer can try an endpoint before writing a line of code.

highlights.title: 5 · Front end · React
highlights.summary: The client is a consumer of its own public API: every screen is assembled from the documented endpoints, with state and actions covered by Jest tests.

highlights.title: Deployed, not demoed
highlights.summary: Front end on Netlify, API on Render, database on TiDB: three separate services, all live and reachable today.

result: Not a site with a database behind it but a public API with a reference front end. The scraping, the schema, the endpoints, the documentation and the UI are one person's work, and every layer is still live.
diagramAlt: Architecture diagram: the official Jelly Belly site is scraped by a Python script using Selenium and BeautifulSoup, which outputs JSON that seeds a MySQL database on TiDB via EF Core migrations; a C# ASP.NET Core API on Render exposes ten documented endpoints through Swagger; a React client on Netlify consumes those same public endpoints.
